rootCause: Bug 1 (colour absent entirely): `createFrameSequencePlacement`'s StandardMaterial sets `disableLighting = true` without setting `emissiveColor`. Traced through @babylonjs/core's actual default.fragment shader (Shaders/default.fragment.js) and materialHelper.functions.js: `PrepareDefinesForLights` skips the light loop unconditionally when `disableLighting` is true, so `diffuseBase` stays vec3(0) forever. `finalDiffuse = clamp(diffuseBase*diffuseColor + emissiveColor + vAmbientColor, 0, 1) * baseColor.rgb`; with `emissiveColor` (material default Color3(0,0,0)) and `ambientColor` (material default Color3(0,0,0)) both unset, the additive term is 0, zeroing colour regardless of diffuseColor/diffuseTexture. Fix: set `material.emissiveColor = Color3.White()`, which makes the additive term exactly 1 so `baseColor.rgb` (the diffuse texture's own decoded colour) passes through unlit and unattenuated.

Bug 2 (colour present but numerically wrong, uncovered only after fixing bug 1): the frame texture set `useSRGBBuffer: true`. This scene's default ImageProcessingConfiguration has no active tonemap/exposure/contrast, so the material compiles without the `IMAGEPROCESSING` shader define — nothing re-encodes a linearized sample back to sRGB before the framebuffer write. `useSRGBBuffer: true` makes the GPU auto-decode sRGB->linear on sample, and that linear value then gets written out unconverted, silently re-grading pixels Blender already finished (verified analytically: sRGB(60/255)->linear->*255 ~= 11.4, sRGB(120/255)->linear->*255 ~= 47.9, both match the measured post-bug-1-fix readings of 12 and 48 exactly). Fix: remove `useSRGBBuffer: true` from the frame texture's options so the shader's `baseColor.rgb` equals the decoded bytes unmodified, consistent with `decodeFrameBitmap`'s existing 'must not re-grade' contract (`colorSpaceConversion: none`).
